summary: This is an April 1st joke RFC. It defines the NSA (No Secrecy Afforded) certificate extension for X.509 certificates, a satirical way to say that private keys may no longer be secret. It is not a serious specification.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7169 is an April 1st joke document about admitting when a private key has been shared. It proposes a certificate flag and warns readers to treat such a key carefully.

questions: what is the nsa certificate extension
what does the nsa flag mean
subtitle: An April 1st joke proposes a certificate label for keys shared with others.

tldr.problem: This April 1st joke RFC imagines certificate holders wanting to disclose that a private key has been shared with a third party.
tldr.mechanism: It defines a critical X.509 certificate extension with a Boolean value: TRUE says the key was shared; FALSE says it may have been shared but the signer does not want to state that openly.
tldr.outcome: The extension is a satirical proposal, not an Internet Standards Track specification. The document says relying parties should treat keys with the extension carefully.

today: RFC 7169 is an Informational document published on April 1, 2014. It is a joke proposal about a certificate extension, not a serious certificate deployment recommendation.

sections.title: The NSA Extension
sections.content: This April 1st RFC humorously proposes an extension for X.509 public-key certificates. Its name, NSA, means “No Secrecy Afforded.” The document imagines using the extension when an entity has shared a private key with a third party.
sections.plainLanguage: This April 1st joke proposes a certificate label for a key that has been shared. The title expands NSA as “No Secrecy Afforded.”

sections.title: The Boolean Value
sections.content: The extension contains a Boolean value and is always marked critical. TRUE indicates that the key has been shared with a third party. FALSE indicates that the key may also have been shared, but the signer does not want to state that openly.
sections.plainLanguage: The flag has two values. TRUE says the key was shared; FALSE says it may have been shared without openly declaring it.

sections.title: Trusting a Key with the Extension
sections.content: The RFC says that a key with this extension must be trusted with care and that a relying party may decide not to trust it. It also says explicitly disclosing key sharing may reduce the risk that a relying party is unaware of it. The closing line is “Secrecy is hard.”
sections.plainLanguage: The document says to consider carefully whether to trust a key marked this way. It ends with the joke that secrecy is hard.
